lesson.menu_title: Presenting Data -- Charts, Trends and What They Mean
lesson.menu_desc: Narrate the chart instead of reading it -- 35 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 11 -- Presenting Data
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Renato Annunciato | Lesson 11 -- Presenting Data

listenings.text: Every quarter I sit through about forty country presentations, and most of them have the same problem. The chart is fine. The narration is not. A lot of presenters read the chart to me, line by line, as if I could not see it. I can see it. What I cannot see is what it means. So here is what I want. First, tell me what the chart shows, in one sentence: units per month, for the last twelve months. Second, tell me the trend, and the one or two moments where it changed. A sharp rise, a dip, the month it peaked. Third, tell me why. Very few presenters do the third part, and it is the only part I remember. And please, do not put every number on the slide. If you have a great deal of detail, put it in a breakdown at the back. A slide with fifteen numbers on it tells me one thing: this person does not know which number matters.

I train people to present numbers, and there are three small mistakes I hear in almost every session. The first is percent and percentage points. If your market share goes from eighteen to twenty-one percent, it has grown by three percentage points. It has not grown by three percent. That sounds like a detail, but in a room full of finance people, it is the difference between sounding careful and sounding careless. The second mistake is the word less. We say fewer clinics and fewer units, because you can count them, and less time and less growth, because you cannot. The third is speed. When people are nervous, they say numbers very quickly, and numbers are the hardest thing to understand in a second language, even for the native speakers in the room. So slow down on the number, stop for one second after it, and then say what it means. That one second of silence does more work than any slide.

extra_audio.text: This chart shows units per month for the last twelve months, in the South and Southeast. The trend is up: sales peaked in March, dipped in July, and leveled off after that. Most of the growth came from a few clinics in Sao Paulo and Curitiba. So the opportunity is clear: very little of our volume comes from the interior yet.
